subject: Onramp linkage evaluation: PrivateLink vs VPC peering vs site-to-site VPN
messages:
From: Tony Lee <tony.lee@northstar.co>
To: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.com>, NetOps <netops@northstar.co>
Date: 2028-06-01T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: NorthStar - onramp linkage ask (PrivateLink / peering / VPN)

Hi Olga,

Quick context: we're evaluating Redwood Private for a staged on-prem -> VPC deployment. We need a short, practical comparison for three ingress/egress patterns: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN (managed on our side). Key constraints for us:
- Multi-account AWS setup (3 accounts) with strict allowlisting (we need a small set of stable egress IPs)
- Sustained throughput target ~2 Gbps, burst to 3–4 Gbps occasionally
- PCI scope: traffic must not transit public internet unless encrypted and auditable
- Two-site redundancy (east/west) with failover behavior defined

Can you send a one-page matrix with pros/cons, operational impacts, and your recommended primary+fallback pattern? Also call out any changes we need in our network (NAT, ALB/NLB, route tables) and whether PrivateLink supports our multi-account model without additional proxies.

We're hoping to finalize the onramp choice by next week. Happy to jump on a 30-min call if it's easier.

Thanks,
Tony
Tony Lee
Director, Infrastructure
NorthStar Analytics

From: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.com>
To: Tony Lee <tony.lee@northstar.co>, NetOps <netops@northstar.co>
Cc: kimberly_park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-06-01T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: NorthStar - onramp linkage ask (PrivateLink / peering / VPN)

Tony / NetOps,

Thanks — great context. I've attached a compact comparison (onramp_linkage_matrix_v1.xlsx) and pasted a TL;DR below. If we agree on desired failure semantics and egress IP constraints I can convert this to a short MOP (runbook) and a SOW fragment.

TL;DR recommendation (short):
- Primary: PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint) per account, fronted by an internal NLB on Redwood Private control plane. Rationale: clean service isolation, no cross-account route-table sharing, and better security posture (no route propagation).
- Fallback: Site-to-site VPN between customer edge and Redwood edge (managed), used for large failover windows or when cross-region peering would complicate routing.
- Avoid VPC peering as primary when you need multi-account isolation + fine-grained control; peering is simpler but can complicate transitive routing and IAM/service controls for our offering.

Key notes and operational impacts:
- PrivateLink throughput: depends on the NLB and endpoint ENI scale; for sustained 2 Gbps we recommend NLB backed N-1 capacity and cross-account ENI warm-up. Testing needed — we can provide a perf-run plan.
- Egress IPs: PrivateLink itself uses ENIs in your account; to present a small stable set of outbound IPs (for allowlisting) you can put requests through a controlled NAT Gateway (or an EIP-backed proxy) in a central account. We can also place a small fleet of NAT proxies in each region for HA.
- TLS/mTLS: we recommend mutual TLS between your NLB and our connector. It satisfies PCI transport requirements and gives stronger auth than IP-only allowlisting.
- Failover: use Route53 health checks / NLB cross-zone failover combined with VPN tunnels as emergency fallback. Document will include expected connection time to failover and session implications.
- Logging & audit: PrivateLink keeps connections inside AWS fabric; we'll emit connection-level logs to CloudWatch or a central S3 bucket with delivery timing for audit.

Proposed next steps (mutual action plan):
1) Confirm whether static egress IPs are a hard requirement vs preferred.
2) We'll run a 2-hour perf test (small fee/time estimate in SOW) to validate sustained throughput on PrivateLink + NLB scale.
3) Draft MOP for cutover with rollback points and a test plan.

Attachments: onramp_linkage_matrix_v1.xlsx (matrix + short diagrams)

If that's a good shape, I can set up a meeting with our network eng and product to walk the matrix.

Best,
Olga
Olga Petrov
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

From: kimberly_park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.com>, ben_carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-06-02T09:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: NorthStar - onramp linkage ask (PrivateLink / peering / VPN)

Quick internal note — looping Ben for scale details. A couple of clarifying items we should confirm before we send the MOP/SOW: 

1) Egress IP strategy: Tony mentioned "small set" for allowlisting. Do we prefer centralized NAT in a shared security account or per-region NAT with a single prefix per region? Each has operational tradeoffs (blast radius vs. complexity).

2) PrivateLink auth model: we called out mTLS. Do we also need to support token-based auth at the application layer for additional auditability? If so, add to the perf test headroom.

3) Peering caveat: if they ask for multi-account peering mesh to avoid PrivateLink, we should document the transitive routing limitations and the requirement that peered VPCs cannot transit to third-party VPCs without explicit routing.

Ben — can you draft the perf-run steps and an estimate for how many NLBs/ENIs we'd need to keep 3 Gbps burst with headroom in a single region?

Thanks,
Kim

From: ben_carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.com>, kimberly_park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Tony Lee <tony.lee@northstar.co>
Date: 2028-06-02T13:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: NorthStar - onramp linkage ask (PrivateLink / peering / VPN)

Folks — added a few concrete operational items and attached a short artifact (pkg-public-eip-allocation-plan.txt) showing an example public EIP allocation pattern if NorthStar wants a fixed outbound set. Copying the key points inline.

- Perf run plan (short): 1) baseline single NLB + 2 connector instances; 2) ramp to 2 Gbps sustained across 10 min windows; 3) scale NLB targets and add ENIs if packet drops/latency spikes observed. Expect to need 3 NLBs (active/standby/warm spare) for 3–4 Gbps burst with predictable headroom in 1 AZ; with cross-AZ you can reduce per-AZ load but need cross-zone balancing.
- NAT options for stable egress IPs: 1) centralized NAT Gateway (single EIP pool) — simplest for allowlisting but single account management and possible bottleneck; 2) EIP-backed NAT instances per region — more management but reduces blast radius; 3) EIP-proxy (small fleet of proxies we manage in a customer-shared subnet) — gives most control and observability. See attached sample allocation plan.
- TLS/mTLS details: we support client cert pinning on our connector. For token-based app auth we can layer in JWT validation at the ingress; that's an extra CPU cost on the connector. We'll dimension perf-run to include token verification overhead if NorthStar wants it.

Assuming we go PrivateLink primary, we should include a short DR test where we fail an entire AZ and spin up fallback VPN tunnels to see application reconnection characteristics. I can include timing estimates in the SOW.

Ben
Senior Network Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Tony Lee <tony.lee@northstar.co>

Thanks, team — this is helpful and aligns with our risk profile. We discussed internally and want to proceed with your proposed architecture: Primary PrivateLink (per-account interface endpoints + internal NLB), with managed site-to-site VPN tunnels as a documented fallback for major outages.

Action items for Redwood:
- Draft SOW and include perf-run estimate (include token validation overhead as an optional line item).
- Include an MOP with NAT options and recommended EIP allocation (we'll evaluate centralized vs per-region after your recommendation).
- Provide a short DR test plan and expected RTO/RPO for switching to VPN fallback.

I'll loop in Contracts to get an NDA/SOW review going — here's the DocuSign link for preliminary paperwork: https://docusign.com/some-doc-link/ABC123

Appreciate the quick turnaround — let's target a kickoff meeting next Tuesday.
